Braising is a combination-cooking method: the food is first seared at high heat in a
small amount of fat, then simmered slowly in liquid in a covered pot. The initial sear
builds flavor through the Maillard reaction, while the long, low-temperature simmer
breaks down tough collagen into gelatin, which is why braised short ribs or pork
shoulder turn tender even though the cut itself is a relatively tough one.
